items.title: Detecting Errors in Large Language Model Responses: The Incremental Predictive Value of Hidden States
items.abstract: Although large language models support a wide range of tasks, hallucinations remain a major obstacle to user trust. When a model generates an answer, both its internal processing and final output vary with the question. Internal states are often expected to offer richer signals for hallucination detection. However, studies using these states typically report their standalone discrimination performance, while output-side comparisons often use simple baselines with weaker modeling capacity. We integrate output-side information available at inference time into a combined baseline and compare detection performance before and after adding hidden states under identical data splits and evaluation rules. Experiments cover open-ended generation and constrained multiple-choice tasks across different models. Adding hidden states improves AUROC by approximately 0.004 and 0.039 on the two tasks, respectively. Hidden states thus provide additional predictive information, but strong standalone detection performance can still yield only limited additional gains.

items.title: Developing an AI Enabled Salutogenic Leadership Model for Abadan Oil Refinery
items.abstract: To develop a context-sensitive model of artificial intelligence (AI) enabled salutogenic leadership for Abadan Oil Refinery, integrating occupational well-being with the organizational requirements of digital transformation. This applied qualitative study integrated theoretical evidence with semi-structured interviews with 18 academic and organizational experts selected purposively for their knowledge of leadership, management, and AI applications. Audio-recorded interviews were transcribed verbatim and analyzed in ATLAS.ti using open, axial, and selective coding. Two independent coders reconciled disagreements through discussion; the reported Cohen’s kappa was 0.79. Preliminary categories were also reviewed by participating experts. The analysis generated 140 initial open codes and a six-category paradigm model. The model comprised causal conditions, intervening conditions, contextual conditions, strategies, a core phenomenon, and anticipated outcomes. Its core combined health-promoting and sustainable leadership, psychological coherence and occupational health, and readiness for human–AI collaboration. Causal conditions concerned leadership relationships, organizational and technological drivers, and attitudes toward technology. Contextual and intervening conditions encompassed health culture, job demands and resources, digital infrastructure, psychological capacities, and digital leadership. Strategies emphasized health support, stress management, leadership development, employee learning, and responsible technological adaptation. Anticipated outcomes concerned employee health and well-being, work attitudes and engagement, and sustainable organizational performance. The model frames AI as a resource for human decision-making within a health-promoting leadership approach. It provides an exploratory framework for refinery management rather than evidence that AI implementation improves health, safety, or productivity. The proposed relationships require prospective evaluation.

items.title: Development and Innovative Applications of Tools for Monitoring Neuronal Electrical Activity
items.abstract: Neuronal electrical activity provides the most direct dynamic readout of excitability, synaptic transmission, circuit coordination, and information processing in the nervous system. Monitoring tools have evolved from intracellular and patch-clamp recordings that resolve ion-channel and membrane currents to high-density extracellular arrays, flexible neural interfaces, optical activity indicators, wireless implants, and artificial intelligence-assisted decoding systems. Each modality captures a different level of neural organization. Patch-clamp recording provides high biophysical precision at the single-cell scale, microelectrode arrays and silicon probes enable population recordings across networks, electroencephalography and functional magnetic resonance imaging support noninvasive human studies, and optical sensors map calcium, voltage, or neurochemical dynamics with cellular or subcellular resolution. Recent advances in ultraflexible electrodes, mesh electronics, genetically encoded indicators, nanomaterials, closed-loop bioelectronics, and machine learning have shifted neural monitoring from episodic measurement toward chronic, multimodal, and intervention-linked systems. This review summarizes traditional and emerging tools for monitoring neuronal electrical activity, analyzes multimodal integration strategies, and discusses applications in disease mechanism research, brain-computer interfaces, neuromodulation, brain-inspired intelligence, and neural engineering. Translation will depend on long-term biocompatibility, stable signal quality, interpretable computational models, and standards that connect device performance with biological validity.

items.title: Development and Integration of a ROSGPT-based Semantic Navigation System with Multi-user Concurrent Tasking under ROS 2
items.abstract: This paper presents a ROSGPT-based semantic navigation system for multi-user autonomous mobile robot (AMR) operation under ROS 2. An environment-specific prompt converts Traditional Chinese, English, and mixed-language requests into structured MOVE, ROTATE, and GOTO commands. JSON-format constraints, station-name whitelisting, and physical-parameter bounds are applied before command dispatch. A middleware mechanism comprising a first-in, first-out (FIFO) Task Queue, a Worker Thread, and a Dispatcher decouples request admission from cloud-based LLM inference and maintains enqueue-order task processing. Validated GOTO commands are dispatched to the Nav2 Action Server, whereas MOVE and ROTATE commands are executed by an odometry-feedback closed-loop controller. The system was evaluated through three experiments covering semantic parsing, concurrent middleware processing, and continuous physical navigation. For a predefined dataset of 150 commands, the Improved Prompt increased the Exact Match Rate from 7.3% to 100%. In a five-client workload comprising 60 requests, all requests completed semantic parsing and structured-command dispatch without observed middleware-level loss. In addition, 39 of 40 continuous physical navigation tasks were completed successfully, corresponding to a task completion rate of 97.5%. These results provide preliminary evidence of the feasibility of the proposed architecture for multi-user semantic navigation in indoor environments.

items.title: Die Entwicklung des Nichtraucherschutzgesetzes in Bayern: Vorbild für ganz Deutschland?
items.abstract: Background: Bavaria is a special case in Germany when it comes to tobacco control policy. The Free State initially enacted a particularly strict law protecting nonsmokers in 2008, relaxed it again in 2009, and reinstated the strict protections following the July 4, 2010 referendum. Research question: Can the Bavarian approach serve as a model for all of Germany, and what opportunities and obstacles arise when applying it to other federal states? Methods: A narrative review based on a targeted literature search, official documents, and two appended texts on developments in Bavaria. The review included political, legal, occupational health, and epidemiological studies related to the protection of nonsmokers in Bavaria and Germany. Results: The body of research consistently indicated that strict smoking bans significantly reduced exposure to secondhand smoke in indoor settings. In German restaurants and bars, fine particulate matter levels dropped dramatically after the smoking ban was introduced, and children's exposure to secondhand smoke at home and in cars decreased without any significant shift to private settings being confirmed. At the same time, the political literature showed that Bavaria's success was achieved only under specific conditions: a simple message, a clear health-based framework, strong mobilization of civil society, and a referendum question that did not hide behind exceptions. Conclusion: Bavaria serves as a model, provided this is understood as an empirically sound and politically mobilizable reference case. The model is of limited use as a blueprint because the federal legal landscape remains heterogeneous and exceptions weaken its effectiveness. The most important lesson is therefore this: protection for nonsmokers is most sustainable where it is simple, has few exceptions, and is justified as a means of protecting the workplace, children, and public health.

items.title: Disclosure Begets Disclosure: A Self-Reinforcing Privacy Loop in LLM Agents with Persistent Memory
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly use persistent memory to personalize responses, and personal attributes in this memory pose a privacy risk if exposed. We ask how consulting memory during dialogue changes what users go on to say, and thus what the memory comes to reveal. In multi-session simulations, a simulated user with 24 personal attributes talks with a support agent that does or does not consult memory, and in both settings attributes are inferred from the full accumulated record. Across four support models, memory raises response quality but also empirical leakage, the share of attribute values correctly inferred from the record, by a margin that widens over sessions. The cause is a loop in ordinary, non-adversarial assistance. Memory-conditioned responses carry earlier values forward, often as presuppositions, and users affirm them or leave them uncorrected, so that cues and the agent's own guesses become recorded values. The loop reinforces itself, and removing the agent's mentions of an attribute lowers its later disclosure about twice as much as single-turn effects predict. Users cannot leave it on their own, since correcting a value discloses the attribute, declining to discuss it shifts later predictions toward sensitive values, and incorrect values left in place become entrenched. The loop is best weakened at the agent's response. Instructing the agent not to state or presuppose attributes brings leakage to about the no-memory level while keeping most of the quality gains, whereas filtering or anonymizing what users say or what is stored gives up much of them.

items.title: DIVE: Benchmarking Full-Duplex Interaction with Visual Engagement in Continuous Streams
items.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have substantially improved spoken interaction and video understanding. Existing online and streaming benchmarks primarily assess causal multimodal perception through timestamped question answering, whereas real-world interaction requires models to continuously identify task-relevant multimodal cues and decide whether, when, and how to respond. This leaves open how well current models can sustain real-time interaction throughout an evolving multimodal stream. To address this gap, we introduce DIVE, a benchmark for evaluating full-duplex interaction with visual engagement under continuous and realistic multimodal streams. It organizes six tasks into three complementary interaction scenarios. (1) Proactive Intervention evaluates whether models can identify emerging visual or semantic cues and intervene at the appropriate moment. (2) Continuous Engagement evaluates sustained participation through continuous visual tracking and visually grounded query interaction. (3) Interaction Coordination evaluates how models coordinate listening and speaking under overlapping and multi-party interactions. DIVE contains 525 audio/video samples with fine-grained human annotations and precise temporal metadata. Its evaluation protocol separates response quality, participation decisions, and response timing. We evaluate representative real-time models using response quality, window response rates, and reaction latency. Experiments show that leading real-time models achieve sub-second average response latency, yet their average window response rates remain at or below 53.77%. Response quality varies substantially across models and tasks, with adapting ongoing responses to newly arriving information remaining particularly challenging. We hope DIVE facilitates progress toward more natural and capable real-time multimodal interactive systems.

items.abstract: Research Hypothesis 1.Nucleus accumbens medial shell (NAcMedSh) dopamine (DA) specifically encodes 1s-synchronized successful cooperative actions, not social contact, motor execution, reward expectation or sensory cues. 2.Learned cooperation-related DA representations have asymmetric stability: they persist after switching to individual tasks, while naive animals need de novo learning for cooperation tasks. 3.NAc D1 receptor (D1R)-mediated phasic DA is necessary for cooperative behavior, with task-specific effects: low-dose D1R blockade selectively impairs cooperation without affecting basal locomotion or individual reward-seeking. items.title: Dynamic Risk Prediction of Patient Clinical Deterioration Using Time-Aware Explainable Machine Learning
items.abstract: The early identification of clinical instability is important in intensive care because such clinical instability usually occurs along a trajectory of abnormalities but not just one abnormal value. The authors designed a time-aware explainable machine learning system that calculates every four hours the deterioration risk based on the previous 24 hours' electronic health records and predicts a new invasive mechanical ventilation, administration of vasopressors, or death in 12 hours. Time-varying vital signs, lab results, treatments, frequency, and missingness are converted into level, variability, trend, change, and recency features and analyzed using LightGBM. The treeSHAP algorithm connects subsequent predictions with changes in the patient's risk factors. The internal performance was AUROC 0.901 ± 0.005 and AUPRC 0.428 ± 0.013 in contrast to latest-value LightGBM AUROC 0.867 ± 0.006 and AUPRC 0.356 ± 0.012. In external validation, the authors obtained AUROC 0.872 ± 0.006, Brier Score 0.078 ± 0.003, and warning lead time 7.6 ± 2.9 h. Dynamic SHAP analysis revealed a pattern that the increased respiratory rate, decreasing mean arterial pressure, elevated lactate, and neurological impairment are common before a prolonged increase in risk.

items.title: Eco-Environmental, Health and Socio-Economic Perspectives on Cyanobacteria and Cyanotoxins
items.abstract: Cyanobacteria, or blue-green algae, the first oxygenic photosynthetic organisms on Earth, play indispensable ecological roles as primary producers and drivers of biogeochemical cycles, and are also sources of human food, nutraceuticals, and biotechnological products. However, cyanobacterial harmful algal blooms (CyanoHABs), intensified by eutrophication and global climate change, threaten water quality, biodiversity, and human health due to their production of diverse secondary metabolites, i.e., taste and odor (T&O) compounds and cyanotoxins. This Special Issue, “Ecology and Toxicology of Cyanobacteria and Cyanotoxins”, compiles 13 papers from 9 countries that collectively advance our understanding of these issues across multiple scales. Cyanotoxins, including microcystins, cylindrospermopsins, anatoxins, and saxitoxins, can cause various hazards to animals and humans, including systemic toxicity, hepatotoxicity, genotoxicity, carcinogenicity, reproductive/developmental toxicity, neurotoxicity, immunotoxicity, and endocrine disruption. CyanoHABs are governed by complex bottom-up and top-down regulation, and blooms and cyanotoxin production are closely linked, but not always consistent/synonymous. Environmental stressors, e.g., phosphorus limitation, cold shock, and grazing pressure, selectively favor toxigenic genotypes, or can increase the cellular cyanotoxin quota, although overall population growth is suppressed. This can be explained by the fact that cyanotoxins can help cyanobacteria to better adapt to environmental stressors. When blooms disperse, demise, or are disrupted by certain interventions, the reduced biomass may increase exposure to dissolved, extra-cellular cyanotoxins if intra-cellular toxins are released faster than they are degraded or removed. We term the uncoupling of biomass and toxicity as the “cyanobacterial biomass–toxicity paradox”. We propose a “3P framework”, i.e., prediction, prevention, and prioritization, for the evidence-based risk management of CyanoHABs and cyanotoxins. We also advocate for more studies using multi-omics and artificial intelligence, as well as multi-disciplinary, multi-sectoral, and multi-stakeholder collaboration under the “One Health” umbrella to translate science into actionable solutions for sustainable development.

items.title: Effect of AI authorship disclosure on purchase intention in cultural tourism souvenirs: The mediating roles of perceived effort and authenticity
items.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) expands in cultural tourism souvenir design and disclosure policies evolve, evidence remains limited on how AI authorship disclosure shapes responses across nationality groups and products. Drawing on signaling theory, two studies compared consumers from China and the U.S. across three disclosure conditions: unlabeled, human–AI co-created, and AI-generated. Study 1 used tourism postcard stimuli ( N = 1110), and Study 2 used mug and tourism tote bag stimuli ( N = 1255). Both studies found that disclosure affected purchase intention and interacted significantly with nationality. Differences across disclosure conditions were significant among participants from the U.S. but not among those from China. In Study 1, the unlabeled and human–AI co-created conditions did not differ, and both exceeded the AI-generated condition. In Study 2, the unlabeled condition exceeded both disclosed conditions for both products, whereas the latter two did not differ. AI-generated disclosure was consistently associated with lower purchase intention than no disclosure, whereas the relative position of human–AI co-created disclosure differed between studies. Parallel mediation analyses showed indirect effects through perceived effort and perceived authenticity. Perceived effort effects were significant for both comparisons with the unlabeled condition across three examined products, whereas the human–AI co-created versus unlabeled authenticity effect was nonsignificant in Study 1 but significant in Study 2. Nationality moderated some, but not all, indirect effects. Thus, firms should not assume that human–AI co-creation enhances responses and should consider clarifying human contribution and pretesting disclosure strategies across products and national markets.

items.title: Embodock: A robust embodied language-driven framework for vision-based AUV docking in turbid waters with zero-shot generalization
items.abstract: Autonomous Underwater Vehicle (AUV) docking in turbid, unstructured environments demands deliberative reasoning beyond reactive pixel-to-action mappings—existing geometry-based and end-to-end learning methods fail when visual features degrade or unforeseen scenarios occur. This paper proposes Embodock , an embodied language-driven framework that introduces Large Language Models (LLMs) as a cognitive core within a closed-loop Perceive-Reason-Act-Observe cycle. We formalize the docking task as a structured decomposition f = f act ∘ f reason ∘ f perceive and introduce three specific technical innovations: (i) a semantic persistence mechanism that maintains operational intent during visual dropout through structured token history; (ii) a vision-dominant multimodal prompt grammar that encodes temporal decision history and auxiliary telemetry alongside visual tokens, enabling context-aware compensation for external disturbances; and (iii) a three-tier Sim2Real pipeline combining knowledge distillation and LoRA fine-tuning to adapt foundation models to data-scarce subsea domains. Extensive experiments validate the framework: in simulated turbid waters ( c = 1.5 m −1 ), Embodock achieves a 92.5% docking success rate with graceful degradation, while real-world lake trials under controlled project-acceptance conditions demonstrate a 4.1 cm terminal Mean Arrival Error and zero-shot transfer to the tested unseen docking geometry; component-level ablations attribute these gains to the three contributions individually.

items.title: Empirical Evaluation of Post Hoc Interpretability Methods for Clinical Trust in Deep Learning Diagnostics
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Brain tumor classification from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has been significantly improved through deep learning techniques; however, the lack of interpretability remains a major challenge for clinical adoption. Methods: This study proposes an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI)-driven framework for multiclass brain tumor classification using a baseline convolutional neural network (CNN) and four transfer learning models, namely ResNet50, DenseNet121, MobileNetV2, and EfficientNetB0. The models were trained and evaluated on a publicly available brain MRI dataset consisting of glioma, meningioma, and pituitary tumor classes. Their classification performance was assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC), and confusion matrix analysis. To enhance transparency and interpretability, Grad-CAM, LIME, and SHAP were used to visualize and quantify the regions contributing to the classification decisions. Results: Experimental results state that the transfer learning models consistently outperformed the CNN by learning more discriminative feature representations while producing more localized and interpretable explanations. The agreement among Grad-CAM, LIME, and SHAP confirms that the proposed models predominantly relied on tumor regions rather than irrelevant background information, thereby improving the interpretability and reliability of the diagnostic predictions. Conclusions: The proposed framework provides an effective and explainable computer-aided diagnosis system that supports trustworthy deep learning-based brain tumor classification and has the potential for decision-making.

items.title: Empowerment of Islamic Religious Education Teachers through Generative AI Training for the Development of Islamic Value-Based Learning Media at SMP Negeri 35 Medan
items.abstract: The development of artificial intelligence (AI) technology, particularly Generative AI, has created new opportunities for developing innovative, interactive, and contextual learning media. However, many Islamic Religious Education (IRE) teachers still have limited competencies in utilizing this technology as a learning medium while maintaining Islamic values. This Community Service Program (PKM) aimed to improve the competence of IRE teachers at SMP Negeri 35 Medan in utilizing Generative AI to develop creative, effective, and Islamic value-based learning media. The program employed a Participatory Action Learning approach consisting of needs identification, educational sessions, practical training, mentoring, and evaluation. The training involved demonstrations and hands-on practice using various Generative AI platforms, including ChatGPT, Canva AI, Gamma AI, and Microsoft Copilot, to develop teaching materials, presentations, assessment questions, and visual learning media based on Islamic values. The results indicated an improvement in participants' understanding of Generative AI, enhanced skills in developing digital learning media, and increased awareness of the ethical use of AI from an Islamic perspective. The teachers were able to produce learning media that were more engaging, interactive, contextual, and supportive of the implementation of the Merdeka Curriculum. This program contributed positively to improving teachers' digital literacy while strengthening the integration of technology and Islamic values in the IRE learning process.

items.title: Engineered human Argonaute 2 for targeted C-to-U RNA base editing
items.abstract: Tools for manipulating RNA that rely on nonhuman proteins, such as ISC-based and Cas-based scaffolds, can lead to unintended and little-understood effects on human cells and present challenges in therapeutic translation. Replacing them with human proteins engineered for expanded, programmable functions could bypass the limitations of these foreign proteins. Here we demonstrate that human Argonaute 2 (AGO2) can be repurposed as a modular RNA targeting domain. AGO2 fused to a C-to-U deaminase enables AGO-led targeted editing of RNA (ALTER). Using guide RNAs that remodel target RNA structure for selective editing and reduced nuclease activity, we show that ALTER achieves, on average, 1.9-fold higher C-to-U editing on mRNA targets in HEK293T cells compared with Cas13 editors CURE and RESCUE. Transcriptome-wide RNA-seq revealed similar or lower levels of off-target editing compared to the same Cas13-based editors. Machine learning models predict that far fewer immunogenic peptides will result from ALTER and we show that ALTER is amenable to a validated workflow for artificial intelligence-directed deimmunization. Human Argonaute is repurposed for RNA editing.

items.title: Engineering Controlled Drug Delivery Systems: Design Strategies, Release Kinetics and Emerging Therapeutic Perspective
items.abstract: Controlled pharmaceutical delivery systems (CDDSs) have progressed from traditional sustained-release formulations to engineered platforms with the ability to modulate drug release in a spatial, temporal and physiological or externally applied stimuli-responsive manner. Recent advances in biomaterials, nanotechnology, microfabrication, additive manufacturing, and bioengineering have enabled precise control over drug loading, transport, degradation, and therapeutic exposure. This review critically discusses the engineering principles that govern the design of CDDSs with special emphasis on polymer selection, carrier architecture, drug-material interactions, surface engineering, encapsulation strategies and physicochemical parameters influencing release performance. It covers the basic and sophisticated drug-release mechanisms including diffusion, dissolution, swelling, erosion, degradation, osmosis and stimuli-responsive release. It also covers the mathematical models to describe and forecast release kinetics. Emerging platforms, such as long-acting injectable and implantable systems, nanocarriers, microneedles, 3D-printed dosage forms, mechanically and remotely triggered systems, and smart responsive carriers, demonstrate the potential of personalized and on-demand therapy. Scalability, reproducibility, biocompatibility, stability, regulatory considerations and patient-centric design are taken into consideration in translating engineered delivery platforms from laboratory-scale development to clinical application. Finally, the combination of artificial intelligence, machine learning, advanced manufacturing and precision medicine is discussed as a potential pathway to rationally optimize drug release and therapeutic outcomes

items.title: Enhancing Adolescents' Physical Education Self Efficacy Through Artificial Intelligence Supported Feedback
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence can provide individualized movement information at a frequency that is difficult to achieve through teacher observation alone. This study examined whether AI-supported corrective feedback could strengthen adolescents' physical education self-efficacy while improving movement execution. Eighty-four students aged 13–15 completed an eight-week controlled experiment involving bodyweight squats, forward lunges, and countermovement jumps. The AI group received pose-estimation-based feedback generated with MediaPipe Pose Landmarker and OpenCV, whereas the control group received standardized teacher feedback. The AI group increased self-efficacy from 4.17 ± 0.62 to 5.39 ± 0.56 points, compared with 4.19 ± 0.60 to 4.66 ± 0.61 in the control group, producing a significant group × time interaction, F(1,82) = 42.31, p < .001, ηp² = .340. Movement scores increased from 64.1 ± 6.8 to 82.3 ± 5.7 in the AI group. Within the AI condition, movement-score improvement and feedback engagement jointly predicted post-intervention self-efficacy, adjusted R²=.487. The findings indicate that interpretable, attempt-specific AI feedback can make mastery progress more visible and support both technical learning and efficacy beliefs in adolescent physical education.

items.title: Enhancing Bug-Exposing Test Generation via Step-Level Credit Assignment and Self-Distillation from Valuable Failures
items.abstract: Large Language Models have shown strong code generation capabilities, yet their outputs often contain subtle bugs. Automatically repairing such code requires informative tests: inputs that expose faulty behavior, paired with correct expected outputs. Recent RL-based test generation methods apply the same outcome reward to all reasoning steps, which can discourage useful reasoning and reinforce flawed steps. They also fail to effectively learn from trajectories that find bug-triggering inputs but predict incorrect outputs, leaving their verified bug-triggering progress insufficiently exploited. To address these limitations, we propose SCALF, a process-supervised RL approach that combines Step-level Credit Assignment with targeted Learning from valuable Failed trajectories. SCALF derives step-specific advantages from process rewards, allowing each reasoning stage to receive its own learning signal. It further routes trajectories that expose bugs but predict incorrect outputs to on-policy self-distillation, using execution feedback to learn from their valuable bug-triggering progress. Across three benchmarks, SCALF outperforms strong prompting and post-training baselines by up to 2.97, 5.26, and 3.53 percentage points in joint success rate, output correctness rate, and bug-triggering rate, respectively. Our code and datasets are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SCALF-F4D1.

items.title: Enhancing Democratic Listening in Online Discussions: The Role of Reaction Buttons, Discussion Moderation, and Large Language Models
items.abstract: Political communication research in general - and research on political online discussion in particular - has focused on the exercise of democratic voice and thus largely neglected the complementary practice of democratic listening. Against the backdrop of a wide-spread perception that democratic listening is lacking in online discussions, we investigate whether listening can be strengthened through novel platform affordances. We developed an experimental chat discussion platform with listening-oriented reaction buttons and created a listening-oriented discussion moderation bot based on ChatGPT-4. We then conducted an experiment involving N=760 respondents in 40 half-hour discussion groups (N=4,466 comments) covering three experimental conditions and a control condition. We compare the effect of (1) listening-oriented reaction buttons versus (2) a combination of these buttons and the listening-oriented human discussion moderation versus (3) a combination of buttons and AI moderation, on the level of democratic listening in discussants’ textual contributions. We show that provision of the listening-oriented buttons does not enhance democratic listening, but that the addition of listening-oriented (human or AI) discussion moderation boosts in-text listening by 5 to 6 percentage points compared to the control condition (21% vs 26% and 27%, respectively). Crucially, we found no statistically significant difference in the level of democratic listening between human and AI moderation. items.title: Enhancing language learning with AI: the role of AI service quality in learning satisfaction and performance in mobile-assisted language learning applications
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-powered mobile-assisted language learning (MALL) applications are transforming the traditional language learning paradigm by leveraging AI technologies to provide a more efficient, convenient, and personalized learning experience. Despite the integration of AI technologies into MALL applications, prior studies have overlooked the critical role of AI service quality in shaping learners’ learning satisfaction levels and performance within these applications. This study addresses this research gap by leveraging social support theory to develop a research model that examines how the AI service quality of AI-powered MALL applications influences social support, specifically informational, emotional, and appraisal support. These forms of support are further analyzed to determine their effects on learners’ learning satisfaction levels and performance. A total of 978 valid samples were collected from users of AI-powered MALL applications and analyzed using the partial least-squares method. The results indicate that AI service quality significantly enhances users’ perceptions of informational, emotional, and appraisal support. These forms of support positively influence learning satisfaction and learning performance. Furthermore, the mediation analysis revealed that informational, emotional, and appraisal support act as partial mediators in the relationships between AI service quality and learning satisfaction and between AI service quality and learning performance. This study contributes to the literature by revealing how AI service quality, social support, and learning satisfaction and performance interact in the context of AI-enabled MALL applications. We also offer practical insights for improving the user experience and maximizing the learning outcomes of AI-driven MALL applications.

items.title: Enhancing the validity of probability prompts using four generative artificial intelligence tools
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (genAI) has become a large influence on students and teachers in the mathematics classroom. Specifically, researchers found that genAI tools could solve probability questions such as “What is the probability of drawing the Queen of Hearts from a standard deck of playing cards on the first try?” These researchers also stated that the genAI tools could not be trusted when solving, “Three cards are lying face down in front of me. Two are face cards, and there are no spades. No card is next to a card of the same color. What are the odds that the card on the left is the Queen of Hearts?” However, it is unclear whether that statement is true. Thus, we verified these findings by investigating four genAI tools (ChatGPT, Gemini, Co-Pilot, and Claude AI) on their ability to complete the identified probability task to determine when genAI can be trusted to perform probability calculation. Using the results of this investigation, we examined these genAI models using their responses and the predictions made by the genAI trainer. The investigation implies that developing mathematical validity requires intentional instruction, including teaching students how to compare genAI’s explanations, conducting GenAI Triangulation Process, cross-checking results using independent methods or alternative tools, and justifying whether an answer is mathematically sound.

items.title: Ensemble-Aware Structural Encoding (EASE): Conditioning Protein Encoders on Peptide Conformational Ensembles
items.abstract: Protein foundation models provide transferable representations for downstream peptide prediction tasks. However, existing representations typically reduce a peptide to a single sequence or structure, which may miss conformational variability relevant to key peptide properties, including antibacterial activity, hemolysis, toxicity, stability, and binding. For example, protease resistance correlates more strongly with conformational dynamics measured by hydrogen exchange than with average helicity. Therefore, we introduce Ensemble-Aware Structural Encoding (EASE), a framework for effectively extracting structural information from conformational ensembles for peptide representation. To extract useful information from noisy conformers, EASE selects central conformers representing a peptide's major structural states and fuses their individual representations with a permutation-invariant operator to produce a peptide-level representation for downstream prediction. We then evaluate our framework on six peptide property-prediction tasks under leakage-controlled splits. Against matched single-structure baselines, EASE improves performance consistently on six tasks with a mean absolute gain of about 3.0% across two structural encoders. Gains keep growing as we add conformers through K=20. A single peptide conformer therefore provides a limited basis for structural representation, whereas our framework distilling and fusing multiple conformers yields a more informative representation.

items.title: Entre la mente y la máquina: hacia una ética responsable en la era de la inteligencia artificial
items.abstract: This article aims to analyze the relevance of cognitive development and comprehensive ethical education in the critical and responsible use of generative artificial intelligence, with the purpose of preventing and counteracting the potential dehumanizing consequences that could affect the human condition in the twenty-first century. From a theoretical-analytical approach, it argues for the need for early digital education that fosters intellectual development and prevents technology from becoming a source of dependency. It highlights that education constitutes a key tool to counter cognitive laziness and the improper use of intelligent systems by university students, to the detriment of their critical reasoning capacities. It concludes that understanding the relevance of brain development and its relationship with cognitive learning processes constitutes an essential foundation for the formation of critical thinking and for the adoption of a responsible ethical approach to the use of artificial intelligence. Integrating these three components –cognitive development, critical thinking, and technological ethics—is indispensable for guiding the application of generative artificial intelligence toward pedagogical and humanistic ends that strengthen cognitive competencies, autonomy, and the reflective capacity of human beings in the twenty-first century.

items.title: Ethical, Legal, and Societal Foundations of AI in Sports Sciences
items.abstract: This chapter establishes the ethical, legal, and societal foundations of Artificial Intelligence in Sports Science, conceptualizing AI as a socio-technical system whose legitimacy depends on fairness, transparency, accountability, and respect for athlete autonomy. It critically examines the implications of algorithmic bias, data imbalance, and limited generalizability, demonstrating how AI systems may unintentionally reinforce structural inequalities across gender, age, and performance levels. The chapter further addresses the “black box” problem and emphasizes the importance of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods in enhancing transparency and trust in high-stakes decision-making contexts such as injury prediction, talent identification, and performance evaluation. Particular attention is given to power asymmetries between athletes and institutions, highlighting risks related to data ownership, surveillance, and the erosion of informed consent. From a regulatory perspective, the chapter analyses key frameworks including the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act, with a focus on high-risk AI systems in sport. Through applied case studies, it demonstrates how ethical principles, human oversight, and governance mechanisms can be operationalized in practice. The chapter contributes to the development of responsible AI in Sports Science by integrating ethical theory, legal standards, and applied methodological considerations.

items.title: Evaluating Generative AI Assisted Lesson Planning for Secondary Chemistry: A Critical Review of Planning Quality and Teacher Judgment
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can produce chemistry lesson plans containing objectives, activities, resources, and assessments, but evaluating their educational contribution requires different kinds of evidence. This critical narrative review examines GenAI-assisted planning for secondary chemistry through three objects of evaluation: the written plan, teachers' professional reasoning and revisions, and students' learning. Seven recent chemistry and science education studies provide the principal contemporary evidence, interpreted alongside research on pedagogical content knowledge, chemical representations, and constructive alignment. The synthesis identifies useful planning support while showing why completed templates, teacher perceptions, and classroom outcomes require separate interpretation. Chemistry-specific review should examine the conditions attached to scientific claims, the connections among representations, the reasoning elicited by tasks, and the responses that trigger instructional adjustment. A worked illustration using electrolysis of aqueous copper sulfate demonstrates how these criteria translate into changes to objectives, diagnostic questions, and follow-up teaching decisions. The article proposes a planning-review procedure and a teacher-education assignment that make justified revisions visible through planning records and discussion. Future studies can connect these records with classroom enactment and student explanations while separating AI assistance from additional opportunities to revise. The review positions teachers' transformation of generated materials as the link between the availability of planning support and the quality of the learning opportunities eventually offered to students.

items.title: Evaluating Learning Transitions Between Program Codes Using an AI-Based SOLO-Adapted Methodology
items.abstract: AI (Artificial Intelligence) has significantly influenced and transformed the way teaching, learning and assessment occur. In this era, AI has become the center of discussion and debate among educators and students in programming education. As such, current evaluation systems seek to provide immediate feedback by leveraging AI capabilities. Feedback is important because it gives both the student and the teacher a holistic view of the learning progress. However, there remains a lack of adequate solutions for evaluating and linking prior knowledge to current knowledge (learning transition) in programming education. To close the gap, we developed an AI model (based on the Google Gemini Application Programming Interface (API) and also following Design Science Research Methodology (DSRM)) that evaluates and categorises program code into SOLO (Structure of Observed Learning Outcome)-adapted stages. The aim of the AI model is to evaluate two program codes by comparing the earlier version with the current code to provide informed feedback. High-level categories of learning transitions include progression (improvement), regression (learning has deteriorated), and no learning (stagnation). The model was tested in all 25 possibilities (learning transitions) to assess its capacity on the given synthetic test cases.

items.title: Evaluating LLM-Generated Feedback on Handwritten Mathematics: Feedback Quality and Subsequent Exam Performance
items.abstract: We evaluate the quality of feedback and practice exercises generated by GPT-5.1 from handwritten university mathematics answers and their grades, and examine whether receiving this feedback improves subsequent exam performance. We use six weekly bonus tests in an English (n=343) and a Dutch (n=236) cohort. Tests 1 and 3 used a crossover feedback design; otherwise, all attendees received feedback. To evaluate the feedback, six reviewers assessed 157 messages from three English-cohort tasks using six criteria scored from 0 to 3. The practice exercises received the highest proportion of strong ratings (95.5%), while diagnostic specificity (41.1%) and clarity and tone (33.4%) received fewer. Feedback for the lowest-scoring answers was rated as less actionable, suggesting that these students may need more targeted guidance from instructors. Comparisons of related exam questions showed mixed results, with no statistically significant differences after adjustment across four comparisons. Greater attendance and feedback exposure were associated with higher exam scores, but the contribution of feedback could not be separated from attendance and practice. Our findings show the potential of an integrated framework merging instructor guidance with automated feedback generation to provide personalised learning support at scale.

items.title: Evaluating Prompt Engineering for Large Language Models-Based Translation
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have introduced new possibilities for machine translation (MT) by allowing translation outputs to be shaped through natural-language instructions. However, evidence about how different prompt configurations affect translation quality relative to established neural machine translation (NMT) systems remains limited, particularly for Indonesian–English translation. This exploratory mixed-methods comparative study examines three prompt configurations applied to ChatGPT and compares the resulting outputs with DeepL and Google Translate across six tourism, promotional, and proverbial texts. Translation outputs were assessed computationally using cross-lingual cosine similarity from text-embedding-3-large as an exploratory indicator of semantic proximity and qualitatively through evaluations by three professional translators focusing on accuracy, appropriateness, naturalness, and discourse style. In the observed sample, DeepL and the baseline-prompt condition tended to obtain higher similarity scores for factual tourism texts, whereas contextual- and persona-prompt outputs received comparatively favorable expert evaluations in selected promotional and culturally embedded cases. Contextual prompting also produced additions beyond the wording shown in the source excerpts, indicating a trade-off between rhetorical adaptation and source fidelity. Because the corpus is small, the prompt conditions bundle several instructional features, repeated generations were not documented, and some reproducibility metadata were not archived, the findings are interpreted descriptively rather than as causal or statistically generalizable effects. The study therefore highlights a genre- and criterion-sensitive relationship among prompt configuration, semantic preservation, and functional translation quality, while underscoring the need for human verification of adaptive LLM translations.

items.title: Evaluating Social Reasoning in Embodied Vision-Language Models
items.abstract: Foundation models now serve as reasoning layers for robot teams, but it remains unclear whether embodiment-specialized vision-language models (VLMs) preserve the social-reasoning capabilities of general-purpose VLMs. We evaluate Gemini Robotics-ER on SHREC, a benchmark of real human-robot social interactions, and compare it with published general-purpose VLM baselines. Robotics-ER outperforms GPT-4o-mini on error/competence detection but performs worse on detailed social-attribute judgments; adding a visual frame helps one task while hurting the other. These results suggest embodiment-specialized models may perform differently on social judgments that can be read more directly from observable interaction cues versus those requiring more inference about a person's internal state. Because the comparison spans model families, these differences cannot be attributed to embodiment specialization alone. This matters for multi-robot systems, where a shared foundation model could cause systematic social-perception errors to influence multiple coordination decisions. This work presents an initial evaluation, with broader cross-context and video-based analyses left for future work.

items.title: Evaluating the Maturity of Large Language Models in Applying Machine Learning Algorithms: A Case Study on the Iris Dataset
items.abstract: This study presents a comparative evaluation of traditional machine learning algorithms and state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs) in classification tasks using structured data. The analysis is conducted on the widely used Iris dataset, which consists of measurements from three different flower species and serves as a benchmark in machine learning literature. The performance of classical algorithms, including logistic regression, K-nearest neighbors, decision trees, and random forest, is examined based on well-established evaluation metrics. Following the implementation of these algorithms in Python (Python Software Foundation, Wilmington, DE, USA), their results are compared with the numerical reasoning capabilities of LLMs, including GPT-5.3 Instant (OpenAI, San Francisco, California, USA), Gemini 3.0 Flash (Google LLC, Mountain View, California, USA), Copilot (Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, Washington, USA), and Qwen 3.5 (Alibaba Group, Hangzhou, China). The LLMbased evaluations are performed by providing algorithm-specific prompts and analyzing the generated outputs. The findings indicate that, beyond their natural language processing capabilities, LLMs can achieve competitive performance in structured data classification tasks, reaching accuracy levels between 90% and 97%. Among the evaluated models, Gemini 3.0 Flash demonstrates superior performance by more effectively capturing multivariate relationships within the dataset. Overall, the results suggest that transformer-based architectures can serve as strong alternatives to traditional deterministic algorithms in numerical classification problems, highlighting the evolving role of LLMs as general-purpose data analysis tools.

items.title: EvaOmni: An Evidence-Grounded Benchmark for Audio-Visual Reasoning
items.abstract: Omni LLMs can naturally locate key audio and visual evidence and integrate information across modalities for audiovisual reasoning. Existing audio-visual reasoning benchmarks that mainly rely on multiple-choice questions usually score models solely based on answer correctness, making it difficult to assess whether a model truly forms a reasoning chain from evidence to the correct answer. In addition, textual or unimodal shortcuts may allow models to answer correctly without analyzing the necessary audio-visual evidence, further weakening the reliability of evaluation benchmarks. To address these issues, we introduce EvaOmni, an evidence-grounded benchmark containing 392 videos and 1,027 purely human-annotated question-answer pairs, covering 15 capabilities and three levels: retrieval and localization, basic understanding, and complex reasoning. We design a series of rigorous annotation procedures in which experts annotate audio and visual evidence and construct video-based distractors; humans review whether questions meet strict inspection criteria, and finally models filter textual and unimodal shortcuts. Beyond high-quality question-answer pairs, we require models to simultaneously return the answer and supporting evidence intervals in order to evaluate the complete reasoning chain. We propose the Coverage Grounded Score (C.G.) to measure how much annotated evidence a model identifies, and the Bottleneck Grounded Score (B.G.) to penalize poor temporal localization in either modality; both are incorporated into answer correctness. Across 7 open-weight and 17 proprietary Omni LLMs, Gemini3.7-Flash achieved the highest overall accuracy (79.4%), C.G. (70.8%), and B.G. (35.1%). At Level 3, it reached 79.1% accuracy, but its B.G. was only 12.3%. These results show that even the most advanced models still have room for development in grounded audio-visual reasoning.

items.title: EviDial: When Correct Depression Predictions Lack Evidence
items.abstract: Depression dialogue benchmarks commonly assess models by comparing predicted symptom labels with clinical scale scores. However, a prediction may agree with a benchmark label even when the dialogue lacks enough evidence to justify it. We introduce EviDial, a benchmark that distinguishes label agreement from evidence-grounded assessment. EviDial comprises 382 depression dialogues from three sources and 2,744 participant-symptom cells, each classified as having absent, partial, conflicting, or sufficient evidence. Because evidence sufficiency lacks a directly observable gold standard, we derive calibrated evidence references from multiple judgments using generalizability theory, many-facet Rasch measurement, and random-effects latent class analysis. Our audit reveals that 82.8% of participant-symptom cells lack sufficient textual evidence for the corresponding symptom assessment, with substantial variation across sources. Across model families and prompting strategies, 69.2%-96.9% of predictions judged correct by benchmark labels are nonetheless unsupported by sufficient dialogue evidence. Further analyses show that strong agreement among LLM evaluators need not reflect independent evidence judgments, underscoring the need to calibrate automated reference panels. These findings demonstrate that label-based evaluation can overestimate evidence-grounded performance by conflating agreement with clinical labels and support in the observed dialogue. EviDial provides a measurement layer for separating these constructs and auditing LLM-based depression assessment more faithfully.

items.title: Evolution of University Students’ AI Dependency and Creativity in the Technology Diffusion Process: A Four-Wave Repeated Cross-Sectional Study in China
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is rapidly reshaping higher education, yet potential risks accompany over-reliance on these tools. Grounded in Rogers’ diffusion-of-innovations theory, the present study employed a mixed-methods design. Four waves of independent cross-sectional quantitative data (T1–T4, N = 788) were complemented by semi-structured interviews with 20 undergraduate students. Key patterns emerged as follows: (i) Across later waves, the direct association between external regulation and intrinsic motivation attenuated, while the indirect association operating via identified regulation strengthened. The path from identified regulation to intrinsic motivation was the only relationship that demonstrated significant cross-pair differences while satisfying invariance requirements for all three wave-pair comparisons. Because scalar invariance could not be established, this pattern is interpreted solely as a descriptive group-level temporal trend and should not be read as evidence of intra-individual change. (ii) AI-assisted creativity showed the largest and most consistent downward shift: estimates in later waves were significantly lower relative to the T1 baseline, with effect sizes increasing progressively (Δ = −0.391 to −0.549; d = −0.61 to −0.95; all p < 0.001 following Holm correction). This pattern remained largely unchanged after adjusting for gender, year of study, and academic major, and held up in four predefined subsamples as well as under propensity-score weighting. (iii) The linkage between AI dependency and creativity was significantly positive only at T3 and became negative but non-significant at T4, pointing to a conditional, wave-specific association rather than a stable linear relationship. (iv) Observed wave-level differences for AI dependency and intrinsic motivation did not withstand correction for multiple comparisons. Sensitivity tests yielded only two significant coefficients for AI dependency and none for intrinsic motivation; accordingly, these fluctuations are not given substantive theoretical interpretation. Retrospective qualitative accounts provided supplementary process-oriented context: participants reported initial exposure to AI driven by prevailing social trends, sustained use based on perceived utility, subsequent disappointment in unreliable or misleading outputs, and eventual shifts toward more strategic, self-regulated engagement. Given their retrospective nature, interview narratives were not used to triangulate or validate the quantitative findings. Collectively, this work suggests that as AI-supported learning becomes normalized within a diffusion-driven context, group-level indicators of students’ subjective creative experiences tend to decline. Higher-education institutions may therefore prioritize protecting learners’ creative agency as an explicit educational goal.

items.title: Evolving Agent Interfaces
items.abstract: Computer-use agents are limited by the interfaces humans give them. An agent may type a spreadsheet cell by cell when a single line of code would do, or print all two thousand lines of a file through a shell to find one function. Both the interfaces and the knowledge of when to use each are built by hand, which cannot keep pace with new applications, workflows, and models. We argue that interface design should itself be an agent capability. We introduce Agent S4, an autonomous computer-use scientist that builds Evolving Agent Interfaces from task experience. A meta-agent examines task agents' trajectories on synthetic training tasks, without success labels, and constructs and revises interfaces and usage knowledge in a repository. Population-based evolution then selects which repositories to develop further by their performance on validation tasks the meta-agent never sees, favoring changes that generalize beyond the seen tasks. On OSWorld V2, Agent S4, with Qwen3.8-27B and the evolved repository of interfaces, sets a new state of the art in open-source computer-use agents, reaching 21.3% binary score, 3.8 times the same model with fixed interfaces. This is above both GPT-5.5 (13.0%) and Claude Opus 4.8 (20.6%), at about 4.3% and 1.5% of their respective costs. On ScienceBoard, the evolved interfaces improve the success rate from 41.4% to 58.6% with the same model. These results suggest that useful interfaces can be evolved from experience, making autonomous interface design a source of improvement complementary to advances in models and harnesses. We open-source our code at https://github.com/simular-ai/agent-s.

items.title: Expertise modulates automation bias and sentinel behavior in human–AI collaborative diagnosis of neonatal pneumoperitoneum
items.abstract: Medical AI is often validated under an additive assumption that algorithmic sensitivity and clinician oversight will combine to improve care. We tested this assumption in the high-stakes diagnosis of neonatal pneumoperitoneum, a time-critical surgical emergency. In a multi-reader crossover study analyzing 1750 interpretation events, clinicians reviewed radiographs aided by either a high-reliability model or a systematically error-injected model. We found that high AI reliability paradoxically induces automation bias in trainees, who accepted 52.0% of incorrect suggestions, while offering limited gains to experts. Conversely, when challenged by flawed AI, the three participating neonatologists exhibited a “sentinel behavior” phenotype, correctly overriding 91.7% of errors (Wilson 95% CI: 83.0–96.0%) consistent with increased deliberation; given the small specialist cohort, this finding is hypothesis-generating and warrants prospective replication. We operationalize systemic resilience as the capacity to maintain diagnostic integrity under algorithmic failure and demonstrate that clinical validity depends on the human–AI team’s adversarial resilience rather than standalone accuracy. To mitigate the risk of deskilling and never-skilling, we release an open-source educational sandbox designed to inoculate clinicians against automated errors.

items.title: Explainable AI for Detecting Safety Barrier Degradation from Near Miss Reports
items.abstract: Industrial maintenance generates near miss narratives that may reveal weaknesses in energy isolation, equipment integrity, permit coordination and other safety barriers. However, interpreting these reports requires contextual judgement, and an automated summary can conceal missing evidence or produce unjustified conclusions. This conceptual paper proposes an evidence-linked artificial intelligence framework for identifying reported barrier degradation and supporting accountable human review. The framework combines a controlled barrier taxonomy, source-linked extraction, retrieval from approved site documents, uncertainty handling and verification of corrective actions. Its central research proposition is that the value of AI should be evaluated through the quality of barrier decisions and the completeness of supporting evidence, rather than classification accuracy alone. A staged mixed methods protocol is specified, including expert annotation, temporal and site-separated testing, comparison with simpler methods, a randomised reviewer study and a prospective shadow deployment. Primary outcomes concern detection of expert-adjudicated barrier concerns, unsupported assertions and reviewer decision quality. Incident reduction is reserved for later investigation and is not inferred from report processing performance. No field dataset, implemented prototype or empirical results are presented. The contribution is a testable research design that connects explainable AI with practical safety assurance while retaining operational authority with competent personnel

items.title: Explainable AI for Sport Scientists
items.abstract: This chapter examines the role of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) in Sports Science, addressing the growing need for transparency, interpretability, and trust in data-driven decision-making. As machine learning and deep learning models become increasingly complex, their opacity presents significant challenges for practitioners working in performance analysis, injury prevention, and athlete management. The chapter conceptualizes interpretability as a continuum and introduces XAI as a methodological framework that complements predictive accuracy with human-understandable explanations. The chapter systematically presents key approaches to explainability, distinguishing between inherently interpretable models and post hoc explanation techniques such as SHAP, LIME, and Integrated Gradients. It further discusses emerging paradigms, including neuro-symbolic Artificial Intelligence, which aim to integrate data-driven learning with structured domain knowledge. Beyond methodological considerations, the chapter highlights the practical value of XAI in enhancing trust, supporting decision-making, enabling model debugging, ensuring compliance with ethical standards, and facilitating knowledge discovery. Through applied case studies in football and basketball, the chapter demonstrates how XAI methods can be operationalized in real-world sport contexts to improve injury-risk monitoring and tactical analysis. Overall, XAI is positioned as a foundational component of Responsible Artificial Intelligence, enabling more transparent, interpretable, and ethically grounded applications in sports analytics and performance modelling.

items.title: Explainable Decision Graphs for Trustworthy Autonomous Multi-Agent Systems
items.abstract: Autonomous Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) are in-creasingly being considered for critical applications such as healthcare, finance, cybersecurity, and autonomous transporta-tion. These systems consist of multiple intelligent agents that can independently perceive information, reason about their environment, communicate with other agents, and execute deci-sions. Although multi-agent architectures provide flexibility and scalability, their distributed decision-making process can make the overall system difficult to understand, audit, and verify. Existing Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques such as Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) primarily fo-cus on explaining individual machine-learning predictions. They provide limited support for representing collaborative reasoning, inter-agent communication, conflicts, and collective decisions. This paper proposes an Explainable Decision Graph (EDG) framework for representing the reasoning process of autonomous multi-agent systems in a structured and interpretable form. The proposed framework models agents, observations, evi-dence, communications, intermediate decisions, conflicts, verifi-cation events, and final actions as interconnected graph com-ponents. A verification layer enables decision pathways to be examined against predefined safety and policy constraints. The resulting graph can provide different levels of explanations for end users, developers, and auditors. The paper defines an experimental methodology using multi-agent execution traces and proposes evaluation through ex-planation fidelity, completeness, decision traceability, human comprehensibility, decision accuracy, explanation consistency, and computational overhead. Empirical numerical results are intentionally reserved for the implementation and evaluation stage.

items.title: Exploring pre-service teachers’ conflict resolution strategies and decision-making patterns in AI-based multi-agent environments
items.abstract: Conflict resolution is essential for teachers. Pre-service teachers (PSTs) often struggle to connect coursework with classroom practice, especially in multi-role conflicts. Artificial intelligence (AI) simulations may offer a low-risk environment. This study examined PSTs’ conflict-resolution practices in an AI-based multi-agent setting where virtual participants were available within the same conflict scenario. We developed a chatbot through which 20 PSTs interacted with an aggressor, an accomplice, a victim, parents, and a tutor in a peer-conflict scenario. Using dialogue logs, we applied inductive qualitative content analysis and lag sequential analysis to examine behavioural transitions. The analysis identified two complementary findings. First, PSTs’ strategies varied by student-agent role. When addressing aggressors, they tended to use guiding reflection, emotional support, surface threat, and role endowment; when addressing accomplices, they more often used positive encouragement, guiding reflection, home-school collaboration, and emotional support; and when addressing victims, they relied on home-school collaboration, positive relationship guidance, and emotional support. items.title: Fact construction as a missing layer in legal AI: a practice-grounded framework for evaluating multi-agent legal consultation
items.abstract: Legal AI research often evaluates large language models (LLMs) on legal reasoning tasks under the assumption that relevant facts are already structured and available. This assumption overlooks a prior and practically consequential stage of legal work: fact construction, namely the transformation of incomplete, fragmented, and interactionally disclosed information into coherent factual narratives. This study conceptualizes fact construction as a distinct evaluation layer in legal AI and introduces a practice-grounded framework for assessing it in AI-assisted legal consultation. Rather than proposing a legal advice system or doctrinal rule-matching architecture, we use a role-separated multi-agent workflow consisting of a fact-constrained Litigant Twin, a structured-questioning LegalAider, a NarrativeAgent for factual synthesis, and an Evaluator for factual-alignment assessment. Using 100 de-identified legal clinic consultation records, we evaluate multiple LLMs under rubric-based assessment, comparing generated factual narratives against original human-authored consultation records in terms of factual accuracy, completeness, and consistency. The results show that LLM-based agents can generate usable factual narratives under constrained conditions, particularly when cases are internally consistent, limited to a single dispute, and supported by clear actor-role relationships. However, cross-model evaluator agreement remains moderate, and outlier analysis reveals recurring structural sources of failure, including anonymization-induced referential ambiguity, third-party reporting, multi-episode case complexity, and numerically dense facts. These findings suggest that reliability in AI-assisted legal consultation depends not only on model capability, but also on interaction design, data representation, institutional record-keeping, and human oversight. By treating fact construction as a distinct analytical layer, this article contributes a practice-grounded framework for evaluating responsible LLM integration in legal settings and highlights the need for factual grounding, contestability, and human-supervised review before downstream legal analysis begins.
